subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of National Defence. In view of the fact that his announcement of the probable elimination of the frigate program will deal a disastrous blow to employment in Canadian shipyards, can he assure the house that before buying any submarines outside the country he will meet the representatives of the shipyards and their labour unions 28902-5-1191
to investigate the possibility and the advantages for Canada of having these submarines built in Canada by Canadians with Canadian taxpayers' money?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I did not say that the program would be cancelled. I said it was under review before proceeding, and that is the case. I can assure the hon. member and other members of the house that my concern is primarily that the armed forces of Canada will have the very best equipment and the highest operational capacity to carry out those tasks that are assigned to them. In addition, along with other members of the government I am very mindful of the needs with regard to employment and industry in this country, and all these factors are taken into consideration in the course of the review.

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I can assure the minister that all members of the house are very conscious of the same thing. However, the minister has been faced with these two problems now for over two months and I am quite sure that the employees are awaiting a decision. Can he tell us when a decision is going to be made?

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext: I cannot say specifically, Mr. Speaker, but the decision will be made just as soon as it can be done without, at the same time, prejudging or not allowing sufficient time to receive all the evidence on both sides of the argument.

subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question of the Acting Prime Minister. Has he received a telegram dated July 3 from Mr. Rene Barras, secretary of the Lauzon shipyard workers union, protesting against the statement of the Minister of National Defence to the defence committee on June 27 that the general purpose frigate program would be carefully reviewed before being proceeded with? I should like to ask the Acting Prime Minister if he would give some assurance to the house that if any cutback in defence shipbuilding is made it will be compensated for by the building of ships for the transportation of Canadian goods overseas.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: REPORTED INTENTION TO CANCEL FRIGATE PROGRAM
speechtext:
This is in effect the same question which was asked of the Minister of National Defence, but I am grateful none the less to

Inquiries of the Ministry the hon. member for giving me notice of the question. I think I should advise the hon. member that I believe the hon. member for Levis has made representations along these lines to the Minister of National Defence.
I am not aware of the telegram, but I cannot add anything to what has been said by the minister, who has stated that the program is under review. In so far as the last part of the question is concerned, it is hypothetical and until a determination of the question has been made I do not believe it is proper to answer the last part of the question.

speechtext: May I ask a supplementary question of either the Acting Prime Minister or the Minister of National Defence. Will the decision of the government await also the recommendation of the defence committee?

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: PAKISTAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Berthier-Maskinonge-Delanaudiere (Mr. Paul) asked me a question concerning Canadian students who are now in Pakistan. Those students, 37 in number, are attending the fourteenth annual conference of the world university service association, which is being held in that country this year. That is the fourteenth conference of its kind organized by that association which has secured the support and close co-operation of every government and student organization in countries where it has been in operation, and it has received the same support again this year.
The Canadian delegation has been the target of criticisms expressed in rather violent terms in a pamphlet published by a group of Pakistani students. We have received no indication that our students have been subjected to any other form of attack or are in any kind of danger. Nevertheless, I have asked our high commissioner's office in Karachi, Pakistan, to send us a report and I shall make it a point to keep the house informed of any development which might cause some concern.

speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I consider

it a definite privilege to be the first minister presenting his estimates for the approval of this committee. I feel, too, that a considerable responsibility rests upon me, a responsibility which I shall endeavour to discharge. I should also like to say a few words about certain aspects of the activities of the department, and about one such aspect in particular which I think is of considerable interest, namely Canada's policy with respect to the forthcoming round of trade negotiations.
For a number of years we have witnessed in Canada the paradoxical situation of high unemployment together with a large adverse balance of trade on current account. In other words we have been relying upon external resources even though productive capacities have remained unused here in Canada.
While economic activity in Canada has risen considerably in the past two years, the extent of this advance has not been sufficient to bring about a sustained betterment in the unemployment situation. Apart from the usual seasonal variations, the level of unemployment in Canada has changed little during the past 18 months despite an abnormally slow growth in the labour force. On the other hand, Canada's external balance is showing evidence of underlying improvement, and much of the expansion now under way in the economy is attributable to the strengthening trade situation.
A quite substantial improvement in the trade balance is now in sight for the current year. In 1963 to date merchandise exports are up by 8J per cent compared with the same period last year, whereas imports are down slightly. In the latest month for which figures are available there was actually a 5 per cent drop in imports notwithstanding the removal of the import surcharges. Tourist trade is also moving strongly in Canada's favour. As I recall the figures, two years ago we had an adverse balance on tourist account of something of the order of $160 million. In 1962 it was of the order of $50 million, and this year we are looking forward to an improvement such as will wipe out the adverse balance and I hope result in a positive balance on tourist account.
This strengthening in merchandise and tourist trade is, nevertheless, offset in part by adverse movements in certain invisible items including higher interest and dividend payments and rising outlays for various forms of business services. Thus in the last 12 months for which figures are available, namely the 12 month period ending March, 1963, Canada's deficit on all current transactions was still in the neighbourhood of $750 million.
A further substantial improvement in this position, which I hope and believe will come

about, will be necessary for Canada to achieve the external financial strength so basic to a sound and viable economy. A strong current balance position is essential not only to pay our way in the world and to head off the current rise in foreign indebtedness but also for the stimulus it gives to domestic activity. This means that we must strengthen our position in both home and foreign markets. Real and lasting progress in this direction will entail new initiatives on the part of Canadian producers, and it will also-this, I think, is of major importance to the members of the house-require careful attention to every facet of activity having a bearing upon the nation's economic performance.
The Department of Trade and Commerce is keenly aware of its responsibilities in this broad national endeavour. The department's role, as hon. members know, is essentially twofold in character. In the period of intensive international negotiations which lies ahead every effort will be made to improve the access to foreign markets for Canadian goods while retaining fair treatment for producers selling domestically. On the other hand, the promotional arm of the department will be striving in every practical way to help the Canadian businessman to take advantage of opportunities available in international markets.
When we consider trade relations in the rapidly changing world of today we are at once struck, it seems to me, by the need for Canada to respond appropriately to the basic shifts that are taking place in the world around us. Canada is, as hon. members know, a great trading nation. To maintain and improve our prosperity, our standard of living, we must maintain and improve our position as an international trader.
The development of the European economic community and of the European free trade area implies far reaching changes in trade relationships. The movement by the big three world traders, the United States, Britain and the European economic community, toward an extensive tariff negotiation next year has major implications for a country as dependent upon trade as Canada. We can expect keener competition at home and abroad in our efforts to maintain and expand markets for primary products and for secondary manufactures. We should set our sights on meeting this keener competition and on taking advantage of new opportunities and broader markets. I am confident that Canadian industry can respond to new opportunities to secure lower production costs by expanding export sales.
About one fifth of our gross national product is accounted for by exports of goods and services. We rank fourth as a world trader, but what we have to bear in mind is that even though we rank just behind the big
Supply-Trade and Commerce three we have a relatively small population and our share of world trade is only a small part of the total. What is big and vital for us may not seem of critical importance for our trading partners. It is the responsibility of Canada and particularly of the Canadian government in its external trade relations to ensure that our interests are not overlooked and that maximum opportunities are opened for the expansion of our trade. We must always strive to place our weight and influence on the side of the orderly growth of trade on the widest possible basis. We must move forward and help to shape the new conditions for world trade in order to improve our prospects and to avoid the dangers of the re-emergence of restrictionism and the stagnation which is involved in a circumscribed domestic market.
Because of the direction and character of our trade, the position and policies of the United States, Britain and the European community are of particular importance for us. But the world, of course, includes many other countries which are significant markets for our products. We have a large and growing trade with Japan, with other commonwealth countries, and in increasing interest in the market provided by many of what we call today the less developed countries which are spread throughout the world, many within the commonwealth and many outside. We must always be conscious of the need to raise the standard of living in these less developed countries and of the contribution these countries can make to the growth of world trade. I believe that one of the great opportunities which is presented to countries like Canada, rich countries, countries with the highest standard of living in the world, is to assist the less developed countries to achieve higher standards of living. This is not only a responsibility but also a great opportunity.
Our detailed work on ways and means of freeing and expanding world trade is being carried forward under the auspices of the general agreement on tariffs and trade in line with the conclusions of the meeting of ministers of trade of the GATT countries in May, on which I reported to the house on May 24 last. At that time I indicated that the purpose of the ministerial meeting was to come to grips with three major trade problems, the expansion of trade of the less developed countries, world trade in agricultural commodities, and another round of negotiations to reduce tariffs and other barriers to world trade. I reported that the countries concerned agreed to come to the negotiating table and that a start had been made toward resolving many of the current,

Supply-Trade and Commerce complex and difficult problems that emerge in a series of negotiations of this magnitude.
Let me refer briefly to those preparations that more directly affect Canadian trade. Hon. members will recall the nature of Canada's export trade in relation to the nature of our import trade. Although our trade in manufactures is growing and must greatly expand, and I hope will greatly expand, in the main we are still an exporter of primary materials and foodstuffs. These are products for which Canada has already in large part negotiated duty free, low duty or other appropriate access to markets abroad. Terms of access for these products to foreign markets could still be notably improved, of course, and trade expanded, particularly where quotas or other restrictive devices have been applied, but here it is rather a question of maintaining the access we have already obtained and that we have bargained for and paid for.
On the other hand, we are one of the world's largest importers of manufactured goods. It was for this reason that I made it clear that the negotiation plan which had been submitted by the United States, based upon their trade expansion act, and which is applicable to the large industrial exporters, would not yield for Canada the necessary mutuality of trade and economic benefit. I made it clear that Canada would play its part and make concessions commensurate with the benefits we receive. This we intend to do, and our role will not be a limited one.
As I intimated earlier, it is precisely because our range of exports is now relatively narrow, and precisely because we must move forward to expand the range as well as the value of our exports, that we must take full advantage of the opportunity presented by the GATT trade negotiations to improve Canadian access to all important foreign markets and, if I may add, particularly in manufactured goods. I trust that the price we shall have to pay in terms of adjustment of the Canadian tariff can also be negotiated in a way which will make a contribution to the competitiveness and efficiency of Canadian production both here and abroad.
An official committee of the GATT countries which was established by the meeting I attended in Geneva, known as the trade negotiating committee, has been hard at work to elaborate the broad negotiating principles set forth in May by the trade ministers. Another body, the GATT cereals group, has already held meetings to exchange views about arrangements for world trade in wheat and other grains in present international circumstances. This work will be continued and intensified in the months to come, leading to


the major negotiating conference scheduled for May of next year.
We are, of course, also active in other bodies whose work relates to trade and associated matters. We consult regularly and frequently with the organization for economic co-operation and development, with our trading partners of the Atlantic community, and we look forward to welcoming Japan to this important grouping. The OECD is, as the house is aware, a body where many of the industrially advanced countries consult and discuss questions of mutual interest in such fields as broad economic policy, development assistance generally, and international trade problems of various kinds.
We have also recently participated in preparatory meetings in Geneva for the United Nations conference on trade and development scheduled for next year. Further preparatory meetings for the United Nations conference will be held in January, 1964. Canada, of course, has long participated in the work of the United Nations and its specialized agencies which have implications for trade. We have played and are playing a role in commodity agreements concluded at various times under United Nations auspices, particularly the international wheat agreement, and in commodity study groups operating under the aegis of the United Nations such as that for lead and zinc. I had the great privilege last summer of presiding at the United Nations conference on coffee. In the important series of discussions leading up to the United Nations conference on trade, particular emphasis is being placed on ways and means of meeting the pressing trade and economic problems of less developed countries.
As I said when I returned from London and Geneva at the opening of this session, this is to me one of the most significant developments that have been taking place recently in world trade. The less developed countries are eager for developments. They are eager for assistance and they are eager to trade.
May I also comment upon the close contacts we maintain through the usual bilateral channels of trade discussions. We are virtually in day to day contact with our important traditional trade partners such as the United States, Britain and other commonwealth countries, the European economic community, and Japan on matters of mutual interest. I expect that the Canada-United States committee of ministers on trade and economic affairs will be meeting later this year, and at that time we shall be reviewing a range of important trade and related subjects with the United States members, including the participation of each country in

the GATT negotiations and questions of particular concern in the trade between the two countries.
Hon. members may recall that when I was in Washington some weeks ago I proposed that our two countries should do some general studies in the field of energy. I hope that at the meeting of Canadian ministers and United States secretaries we shall move this proposal another step forward. It was well received on an informal basis by the United States secretaries I had the privilege of meeting, and I fully expect we can have a most useful exercise which will have far reaching implications on the development of our energy resources in oil, gas, electrical power, nuclear energy and coal in the years to come. In the meantime, of course, there is a continual interchange between the two countries on trade matters of mutual concern as the need arises or as opportunity for fruitful consultation appears.
In May of this year, at the meeting in London of the commonwealth economic consultative council, I had the welcome opportunity of discussing with British and other commonwealth trade ministers a range of commercial problems of common and particular concern. This meeting was most timely, coming as it did just before the meeting of GATT trade ministers. As the house knows, I was able at that time to have useful discussions with the British minister of agriculture about the important changes pending in their policies affecting imports of farm products. As I said at that time in answer to a question by the Leader of the Opposition, I think the changes that are taking place in British agriculture policy could be very constructive and, from our point of view, they are important and I believe perhaps indicate a way in which relations between importing countries with protective policies and exporting countries like Canada could be put on a more secure basis.
Such bilateral consultations complement the work we are doing in multilateral organizations, in concert with other important importers such as the European community and in concert with other exporters, to establish a satisfactory framework for expanding trade in farm products, which is one of the main problems facing the world in the months ahead. Agricultural trade continues to face greater barriers and obstacles to expansion than is the case for industrial products generally. It is our aim to achieve a framework for trade that will permit of a greater exchange of agricultural goods under conditions which recognize more than at present the desirability of drawing supplies from efficient producers. A parallel aim is to limit
Supply-Trade and Commerce the adverse effects on trade of excessive agricultural protectionism throughout the world in both exporting and importing countries. We are also giving careful consideration to our exchanges with state trading countries. I am hopeful that progressively we shall be able to find a stable market in at least a number of other countries, not only for wheat but for other Canadian products. In return, as with other countries, we must expect to see their goods find a place in the Canadian market under conditions which will not pose the threat of disruption to efficient Canadian production.
Many problems are involved in moving in this direction. I know that some hon. members on the other side have had some direct experience in these matters and fully understand that I am not exaggerating the difficulties. However, I am confident that, given the desire on both sides to do so, appropriate solutions can be found and, if I may say so, have from time to time been found.
In my report to the house on May 24 I indicated that reaching international agreement on the broad lines for future negotiations was by no means easy. I said that much remained to be done before there could be confidence that the various negotiations would yield a substantial and positive result. This is still the case. Under the tariff negotiations committee established by GATT ministers in May, machinery has now been set up to deal as a matter of urgency with such key problems as the depth of tariff cuts and the question of exceptions as between the large highly industrialized countries which are expecting to participate in the tariff negotiations on a linear basis, and countries like Canada which will be participating on the basis of an exchange of concessions of mutual value. By the end of the summer we should have a clearer idea than is possible at present of the scope and character of the tariff reductions that may be negotiated by the United States, the European economic community, the United Kingdom and other European countries, both within and without the free trade area.
It is the intention of the Canadian government to establish appropriate procedures and facilities to enable the government to secure the benefit of the views of all Canadian interests concerned both with respect to concessions that may be offered by other countries and with respect to the Canadian tariff. This will be done as soon as enough information about the scope of the negotiations is available to permit meaningful consultations.
I have had a number of inquiries, and perhaps other hon. members have had these inquiries, about when consultations are to

Supply-Trade and Commerce begin. For that reason I emphasize again that I do not think these consultations should begin until we know enough about the scope of the negotiations to make these consultations meaningful, and to avoid having to undertake them twice. The government attaches particular importance to such consultations as we move into the phase of detailed preparations for Canadian participation in negotiations that may well be of very great importance for Canada's trading position and for world trade.
I am convinced, and I am sure the house will agree, that our posture toward these negotiations should be active and positive and that we should use our influence to shape them in a way consistent with our national interests. In this regard we must obviously be prepared to make a contribution commensurate with the benefits to be received and appropriate to the objective of the further expansion and liberalization of world trade.

subtopic: INDUSTRY
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am sure all hon. members wish to thank the Minister of Trade and Commerce for his first statement in opening discussion on the estimates of his department. I am sure he must derive a certain amount of satisfaction in being one who has gone up the ladder all the way in his department. I am also sure he must now view the whole problem of trade and commerce somewhat differently, now that he has certain political responsibility in regard to the policies and administrative practices of that department.
The minister spoke about the objectives of the trade policies of his government, and I hope we will hear something more about them in detail. Doubtless we will later on, particularly with regard to the nature of the development here in Canada and the degree of co-operation between the government and industry as such. I should like to refer to this in greater detail later on.
I was keenly interested in the remarks of the minister when he was speaking about the deficit Canada faces on its current international account. He must of course realize there has been a changing pattern in this regard since the time he was deputy minister; because at that time, going back to 1952 in any event, one of the significant features of Canada's deficit on the international account was the extraordinarily high and unfortunate deficit on merchandise or commodity account, a situation which has been gradually improved to the point where for the last two years we have had a surplus on that account.
There were various factors which led to this result, and I think the minister would agree that the deficit on international account must be tackled in various sectors over some of

which he has relatively little control. He has inherited a cumulative situation going back for scores of years when Canada always had a deficit on international account. This has accumulated primarily through the investment of foreign capital in Canada, particularly since 1945 when there were extraordinary amounts of foreign capital invested here. We now see that we must pay for that capital by way of dividends or periodic repayments.
I think the minister would also agree with me that before this situation gets better it will get worse, in that as economic activity develops in Canada, naturally foreign owned industry will benefit from this healthy climate, and greater dividends will have to be paid abroad unless there are compensatory fiscal or budgetary policies which would encourage the reinvestment of those dividends in Canada to the point where we might look to a Cana-dianization of this foreign capital. In this regard I feel some sympathy for the minister in that I am sure he is holding his head visualizing the potential effects of certain recent budgetary moves on the level of Canadian trade.
In indicating the bases on which we must be able to sell our goods, first of all they must be of good quality, improved and improving Canadian technology will guarantee that. Second there is the question of active selling; and our businessmen, as a result of the encouragement they have received in the past and I hope will continue to receive, can become much more active sellers. There is nothing so disastrous for our trade policies as having people who expect they can stay at home and that buyers will beat a path to their door. Those days are gone. They have to go out and sell and sell and sell. If they miss out the first time they must go back a second time and even a third time.
Finally there is the question of price. We know that a manufacturer has only certain controls over price. He may be a shrewd bargainer with respect to his raw materials. He may be a very competent administrator and have a very efficient plant, but there is one thing about which he can do nothing and that is the level of taxation he faces, and within the price he sells abroad he must include taxation at the domestic level.
I must say that the recent proposal of the government with regard to the extension of the sales tax fly completely in the face of the objectives of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. This was the hidden dynamite in the budgetary proposals. I am not talking about building materials but primarily the tax on production machinery and on materials entering into industrial processes. We have seen the immediate effects of this.

When I asked a question of the Minister of Trade and Commerce shortly after the budget, he could not give me an estimate of these effects. Two of the main items which enter into international trade are pulp and paper, and we have seen an advance of $7 a ton on pulp as a result of the tax increase on materials going into industrial processes. All the bleaches and industrial chemicals which go into the preparation of pulp and paper have become subject to this tax, and it is bound to follow that everywhere along the line we are going to get a much greater increase than 11 per cent.
If building materials are taxed at 11 per cent, or at least a portion of those that go into industrial plants, and if production machinery and raw materials, which are not identifiable in the end product, are also taxed we are going to get an accumulation of this tax and it will more than exceed 11 per cent. For instance I have been told that in another sector which is very important, our soft woods from B.C. and Alberta, the price will rise by 16 per cent and perhaps more.
I am sure the minister must realize that while the previous administration was faced with some problems with regard to action by the lumber producers of the northwestern United States to get quotas imposed upon Canadian lumber exports, yet as a result of negotiations and representations by the government and other interested Canadian parties such a quota was not established. But with the greatest respect, Mr. Chairman, I think the Minister of Finance has just as effectively established a quota now, and our lumber exporters are going to be faced with precisely the same problem that they would have faced had the United States administration imposed quotas on exports of Canadian lumber. This in effect is going to be the result of the budgetary proposals if they are carried through. However, I am not taking part in a budget debate so I will pass from that point.
The minister indicated, I think quite clearly, that Canada is not a state trader. There is really only one state organization which really participates in our external trade to any extent; that is the Canadian wheat board. We have been very successful with wheat and I trust the minister will see that this success continues, though I have some very grave reservations as to whether the wheat board should be under the aegis of his department rather than where it was, under the Department of Agriculture.
We are faced, and are going to face, greater competition in the international market as a result of our budgetary policies, we are also going to face keener competition in our do-
Supply-Trade and Commerce mestic market. We know some of our problems in the last 15 years were caused by losing the position Canada held in the immediate post-war years. At that time we were competing with countries whose industrial capacity had been either diminished or completely exhausted by the war. We stepped into a strictly sellers' market for a number of years, and unfortunately I think Canadian business and Canadian government thinking at that time was conditioned by this sort of mentality; "You have a free ticket in a sellers' market". Only in recent years have we run into a completely different form of competition, which has not only cleaned us out of many foreign markets with respect to manufactured goods but which came and took those markets away right in our own house, right within our own domestic boundaries.
I realize that trade is a two way commodity, but we have seen time and time again that Canadian industry operating with obsolescent plants could not compete either in quality or price with foreign commodities. Canadian buyers, who are interested like anyone else in obtaining the best goods at the cheapest price, have simply been turning to foreign products. Again, Mr. Chairman, I am rather fearful of the budgetary policies and the effect they will have on the prices of Canadian commodities which are sold within the domestic market.
In so far as Canada is not a state trader, I believe that the best effort which could be made by government would be toward the creation of the appropriate climate for the expansion of our trade. If we have a healthy economic climate we will have industry that is competitive. Undoubtedly the minister will refer to this matter-I hope he will-and will give the house and the country some indication of the government's policy with reference to the continuation of trade conferences at the domestic level or even, shall 1 say, on a bilateral level, rather than these grandiose, ministerial trade conferences which are all very well but which do not sell goods.
I am concerned here with the direct liaison that was established in the past three years between Canada's trade commissioners and Canadian industry. We saw what happened in 1959, I believe it was, and again this spring. These things take some time; we are not going to get miracles overnight, and Canadian industrialists and businessmen are not necessarily going to sell the first time around. But I know from direct reports of businessmen from western Canada-and this is the attitude that seems to be adopted by businessmen in eastern and central Canada-that somehow or other they are not being consulted with regard to the export market because there is

Supply-Trade and Commerce thought to be no great level of secondary industry in that part of Canada. I think this is a snare and delusion, because we have a very healthy and growing level of industry in that part of the country and I am sure it would be in the interest of the government to try and stimulate this industry.
These contacts are, frankly, the most valuable that we can establish. We should also have more trade fairs of the type we had in March and April of this year, where the government of Canada goes out and gets people to come here. We should not adopt a passive attitude in this regard; we have to go out and attract business in this way. We may have to introduce certain gimmicks but the net result, if our businessmen are able to sell their goods, is that the policies of the government are successful. I do not think there is any partisan approach in this regard, but this is what businessmen are looking for; and as far as I am concerned they have been enthusiastic about the relationships with and assistance they have received from the officials of the Department of Trade and Commerce.
In another debate the other day I referred to this matter. I think this is an area in which there is a great deal of scope. A fine start has been made, and it would be a shame to let it either stagnate or diminish. In this area, if businessmen from all parts of the country can come and say "All right, now can you help us with information in this regard?" and if departmental officials and the minister go to different parts of the country and hold regional conferences, as has been done, this would greatly assist our industry. I am sure the minister is fully aware of the value of our trade policies in the last two or three years.
I do not wish to speak about our currency position vis-a-vis other nations or to discuss in a dollar sense the position of this country. It is a fact that the government is not a state trader. There is one aspect of this problem that is often missed by certain commentators on the national scene and people who professedly have free trade interests, who berated the previous administration with regard to the question of quotas. I know it is a knotty problem, but we have to look at the position at home as well as to our economic climate. Are we going to see certain industries completely wiped out by countries which have rather selective policies with regard to exports to this country? I think when we receive complaints from various countries which say they now have a great trade imbalance with Canada on dollar volume, and that they import twice or three times as much from us as we import from them, we must look at the difference in the

population of our country and the country concerned. Having done this, I find it a little difficult to freely accept their observations.
I do not like to single out any particular country, but since certain newspapers have adopted the arguments put forward by certain business interests, let us take Japan. The proposition is put forward that Japan buys from us almost twice as much as we do from them, and that this trade pattern cannot continue. On the other hand Japan's population is some 80 million to 90 million people compared with our 18 million. Since most of the goods entering into trade are consumer goods,
I find it difficult to understand how it can be expected that Canada should more or less arrive at a bilateral balance of trade with such countries.
The same applies to our trade with Great Britain. We are engaging in multilateral trade. We are going to have excesses in some regions and deficits in others in arriving at the over-all picture. So far as commodities coming from Japan and other countries with a lower labour cost element are concerned, we see the effects when the exports of those countries are selective. I think we can certainly work for much more extensive trade with such countries if the trade is on a general pattern covering goods generally, and I say more power to each country if its volume of mutual trade can increase. But we cannot say "All right, our doors are open to you and we will take all you wish to export to us in particular commodities, and we will willingly see our plants close". We have seen textile plants from one end of the country to the other close, as well as plywood factories. These are the facts that are hard to accept so far as the Canadian economy is concerned when we see whole towns made destitute as a result of the closing of principal industries. I think the parliamentary secretary to the minister knows whereof I speak, in particular as to the small textile towns in the provinces of Quebec and Ontario.
There is one further point I should mention in this opening statement, Mr. Chairman, and it concerns the international negotiations now taking place. We saw last year the negotiations which took place with regard to Britain's proposed entry into the European common market. I wonder what the members of the present administration feel at this time compared with their attitude 18 months ago in light of the events which have transpired. 1 was clearly of the opinion after a trip tc France last summer that what turned out to be the ultimate result was bound to come. I think we must fully realize that one of the keystones of the common market is the protection of French agriculture, and unless that

is taken care of to the satisfaction of France there will be difficulties about further participation in the European common market so far as Great Britain is concerned.
There are also many potential difficulties with regard to Canada and its agricultural exports. We have only to see what was the result on American poultry entering into the European common market and is now barred. In any event these are the ebb and flow of trade patterns. The world is not going to come to an end because there is a temporary check due to a certain move having been taken. After all, no one will beggar himself just for the sake of enriching his neighbour so far as trade is concerned. I think we in Canada must do everything to put our house in order so as to be an active competitor, and I do not think we have gone as far as we could there.
So far as entering into the detail of the various trade patterns being developed at the present time is concerned, I think this must be very carefully watched. Canada must at all times indicate clearly and early what it feels will be the effects upon Canada of the trade proposals of other countries. Sometimes the larger trading nations of the world make certain proposals which are all very well for them, but they are not overly concerned about the splash which hits their neighbours. We must clearly indicate that if certain steps are taken it should be realized that this is bound to be the result as the problem affects us, and we must show that there are two sides to every coin.
Leaving that point aside I should like to come back to the last item of which I have made a note, and that concerns tourism. I have always felt pretty strongly about this. It has always been ludicrous to me that over the past few years 18 million people should have spent far more on tourist travel abroad, which is a straight consumption expense with no return to Canada, than the rest of the world has spent in this country. We must be a nation of people who do not like our own homes and have a psychosis which makes us feel that for a month in the year we must get out of here.

The hon. member for Leeds says that we try to get warm. I do not know that that is necessarily so. Last week people were looking for a place where it was cool. I think the Canadian government must develop on a national basis and in participation with the provinces a pattern or program of tourist attraction for Canadians within Canada. Let us have Canadians travelling across Canada for once. True enough, I think a significant step was achieved last year with the completion through the Rogers Pass link of the
Supply-Trade and Commerce trans-Canada highway. But it goes beyond that. I think the government must give encouragement to the development of proper hotel facilities and the development of motel and service facilities in our national parks, or at least close to national parks, particularly the western parks. They are so vast that you just cannot expect people to visit them at express speed, providing no place for them to stay. It is ludicrous to expect people to go to Banff national park, for instance, if they are not to be received properly. The same applies to some of our other national parks, and I suggest to the minister that he might twist the arm of his colleague, the minister of northern affairs, and have this policy apply to some of our other national parks across the country. People must be encouraged to come to the parks and stay there for some time, not just to pass rapidly through them. They might as well take T.C.A. and fly overhead if arrangements are not made to receive them properly.
Today people expect the best of facilities. Canadians are not going to accept second rate or third rate accommodation, even though we are prepared to offer the best to those who come from outside this country. We must encourage our restaurants to cater properly to tourists, to Canadians as well as visitors from outside. The successful handling of this situation would make an enormous difference to our trade balance. I recall that only three years ago our tourist deficit had reached a point where it was only $200 million or $250 million short-this out of a total deficit of over a billion dollars. That to me is incomprehensible when we have such natural advantages which we could turn to good account. I read suggestions in some papers that Canada was wrong to approach the United States with a request that the limit on permitted expenditure on a customs free basis for Americans visiting this country should not be lowered. The suggestion was that we might expect fewer tourists as a result.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
The minister has referred to assistance to the less developed countries in order to raise their standards of living. I think we would all agree as to the desirability of doing this. No one wants charity, least of all the recipients, but I think everyone believes we should give these countries technical assistance and go out of our way to develop trade channels between them and ourselves, even not necessarily on a paying basis in the first year. It should be remembered that though these countries may enter into competition with us in certain fields at a future date, as a result of their rising standards of living they may also become good customers of ours on a reciprocal basis.
In this regard I should like to hear the minister tell us when he replies, either today or on some other occasion, to what extent we in Canada are intensifying our trade pattern with the Caribbean islands. I believe this is an area which has been neglected for scores of years. I speak of not only indirect forms of economic assistance but also of help through the economic aid office of the Department of External Affairs. It seems to me we could have done a great deal more in this particularly sensitive area where we can see the hands of these people tendered toward us. I think there is a natural link between this country and the Caribbean islands but we have been very remiss, content to take a passive attitude. I am not suggesting we should extend at this time as far as South America and Central America; let us recognize the limits of our capacities. But I should like to see us doing much more in this field. I am not blaming any particular administration. I think Canadians as a whole have been neglectful of this area, not only with respect to trade but in the field of education.
I suggest there might also be some relaxation in the restrictions placed on immigration. It seems to me we should be able to establish a much closer contact with the Caribbean islands. More and more Canadians who have visited these islands tell us that for certain reasons Canadians are becoming increasingly favoured in the eyes of the inhabitants. Once there is a feeling of this kind among the general population, it will be found that the response to trading efforts is far better than it may have been in the past. It will take some work, but the results in the end will surely justify it. I think both the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of External Affairs could do more in this direction.
There may be some other points on which I should like to have spoken, but we can


always come back to them. I wish to thank the committee for having given me these few extra minutes.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to make a few remarks on the matter now before us.
First of all, I would like to point out that sometime ago I proposed in this house that everything that concerns distribution of our production should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce; in other words, in my opinion, all products offered for consumption should come under the Department of Trade and Commerce. This is an extremely practical suggestion because, to date, it seems to me that we have not always realized that the Department of Trade and Commerce has a responsibility for distribution and that it must see to it that our national products or production reach the consumer.
We have also noticed that up to now, the activity of the Department of Trade and Commerce has been rather restricted to foreign trade. As a matter of fact, considerable effort was made to open up external markets at a very high cost, because we keep trade representatives in a large number of countries of the world, but I think we can venture to say that we have one at least in every important country, who is trying to find new markets for our Canadian products.
Mr. Chairman, I agree that foreign trade is important, that we must try to increase it, but why not also be concerned with the market here at home.
In fact, those who are not floating above the clouds can see that millions of Canadians live in a destitute condition because of a lack of means and purchasing power which prevents them from buying all they need.
As a matter of fact, if we examine statistics respecting families who live on social welfare or depend on unemployment insurance, we reach a figure of close to 3 million Canadians who do not have adequate incomes to purchase the food, clothing, in a word the articles of vital necessity or who cannot even afford to live in decent accommodation. This is a market which represents billions of dollars and we are not at all concerned about it.
I know that our present financial system production cannot fill all the needs of Canadian consumers. This is the reason why we, Social Crediters, advocate a reform of the present system. We know that we are on the right track. In fact, if someone among us offered a solution that would enable Cana-

dians to take full advantage of production, we would be the first to support him. Unfortunately, the old line political parties have never submitted any serious solution that would enable the financial system to work efficiently.
We are continuously witnessing thousands of bankruptcies which seem to be essential to the proper working of our economic system. Without those bankruptcies, our trade and our financial system would have been paralysed a long time ago.
Mr. Chairman, a little while ago, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), stated that Canada is bent progressively towards a freer international trade and that a conference will take place in Geneva in 1964 with a view to concluding new agreements on tariffs and trade.
Our party fully agrees with the minister, because we feel that we should have freer trade.
It so happens at the present time that our international trade is impeded because we only accept currencies which can be converted into gold and we refuse those of other foreign countries. Trade should almost always be conducted in American dollars, because the American dollar is at a premium over practically all other world currencies. That is why, most of the time, we are in a painful situation, in view of the constant imbalance of our international payments. We are unable to correct this imbalance and we shall not be able to do so, unless essential reforms are instituted to promote our international trade with many friendly countries just waiting for us to open our doors to them.
I remember, for instance, that when the international monetary fund was established in 1944, the well-known British economist, Lord Keynes, advocated the creation of an international currency which would be called the "bancor". It would have facilitated international trade without requiring the abolition of national currencies. An interesting aspect of that suggestion was that the currency would not have been based on the gold standard but would have been put on the market in accordance with the actual needs of international trade.
I truly regret that preference was given at the time to the American theories and that Lord Keynes' proposal was turned down. In my opinion, the latter was a lot better and it would have facilitated international trade a great deal more.

Before too long, and at the proper time, I shall have the opportunity of introducing a bill to further facilitate international trade. At that time, I shall go into the matter more thoroughly and prove that it is possible to amend the Bank of Canada Act in such a way that we could expand our international markets in order to increase our international trade even more.
And now, before I resume my seat, I should like to say, Mr. Chairman, that it should be remembered that Canadians, first of all, want to consume Canada's production. This is a most important point and we shall keep on repeating it in the house. Unless that essential point is understood, our country will remain in economic stagnation, precisely because we do not give any thought to directing our trade in such a way that Canadians can consume our whole production.
Of course, I realize very well that we cannot consume all the products we make. We can, however, exchange them with other countries, but we need the means to do so.
I shall therefore have an opportunity, later on, to speak further about this matter when I present a bill to amend the Bank of Canada Act, precisely in order to increase greatly our international trade in an extremely favourable way.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity, and a very welcome one, for us to discuss the trade policies of the government. I might say, in beginning, we consider this particular department to be an extremely important one, and one we believe will play a very important part in the future of the country. Having said that, however, I hope the minister will not think it unkind if I express some mild surprise that we are proceeding with his estimates today. I would have thought that with the need for internal stimulation of the economy in Canada, we might well have used this day to discuss and pass some of the government's very urgent legislation, such as the municipal loans

Supply-Trade and Commerce measure which is designed to provide a very quick solution of unemployment. I would have thought that, while this is an important department, it could have stood a day or two and we could have spent today passing that very important piece of legislation.
However, Mr. Chairman, there are some comments we would like to make on the minister's opening statement. In listening to him, it seemed to us that the whole of the statement was based upon the concept of freer trade in the world. This was a very popular concept, and still is, and was based upon the idea that the United Kingdom would enter the common market, and it would become a very outward looking organization; that there would be a general and fast move towards free trade in the world. I did not see in the minister's statement anything that really sells us on the idea that this is the situation that exists. I hope that perhaps at some stage someone speaking for the government will make out a case for freer trade.
It seems to me that there are one or two flaws in the argument that perhaps could be answered at some later stage in the debate. The first one would be that with Britain not having gained entry to the common market, there is no evidence at all that the European economic community is, in fact, becoming a very outward looking trade group or one which is genuinely interested in making very widespread tariff concessions. In fact, there seems to be a trend in the other direction. It is tending to be an inward looking, insular organization with a highly restrictive policy, particularly in agriculture, and one which will have a very drastic effect presumably on our ability to get into these markets.
In addition, Mr. Chairman, if you examine the statements of some people in Britain, in particular those of Mr. Harold Wilson, the leader of the labour party, you do not get the impression that their views are wholeheartedly in favour of the fast move towards freer world trade. With the political climate in Britain, it is not unlikely that the labour party will become the government in the near future, and in examining some of the statements their leader has made on the subject one would have some doubts about this theory of freer trade becoming operative.
The other difficulty with the doctrine of free trade, which is basic to the government's position, is that it seems to me you are permitting the forces of laissez faire to dictate your external markets or your external policies at the very time when most world governments are operating on a reverse philosophy within their own domestic economy. By the use of planning, incentives, direction

and control over the economy, they are tending more and more to internal control of the economy. It seems to me you are setting in motion forces which tend to be in conflict within the economy itself. I do not really see how you can have the forces of laissez faire dictating world markets at the very time when most modern countries are exercising a greater and greater degree of economic control, economic planning, in their domestic affairs. This is not to say that the doctrine of free trade is not an admirable one, and perhaps it will mean that this will he the trend. In the minister's speech this morning,
I did not hear anything that really made a case for freer trade. This was a popular doctrine a year ago. World conditions have changed since then. I am just wondering to what extent the government has taken into consideration some of the major shifts in trade patterns that have taken place in the last year.
In his address this morning, the minister told us that the government was prepared wholeheartedly to support the tariff negotiations which will be taking place under the Kennedy trade expansion bill. I think, in general, this is good, Mr. Chairman. Again, there should be several caveats lodged in respect of these negotiations. I think, first of all, we have to remember that the Kennedy initiative has been tremendously weakened in these negotiations by the failure of Britain to gain access to the European economic community. The Kennedy trade expansion bill was almost predicated upon the success of the British application, and her failure to obtain entry means that the impetus behind the Kennedy negotiations will be considerably weakened.
It might well be folly to place too much emphasis on the chances of great success coming out of that particular type of negotiation. We also have to remember that the United States trade expansion act is essentially designed to relieve pressure on the American balance of payments problem. This means that the United States is primarily interested in exporting more and importing less. This is not to cast any particular doubts on its good will in these matters, but it is important to remember that it is essentially an act designed to benefit and further the interests of the United States in world trade.
Third, the real advantage to Canada under this series of negotiations lies in having Canadian products included in the 80 per cent group, which would permit negotiations towards free entry of products from Canada into the United States and areas of Europe. With these not being included in this group, then the degree of benefit we will obtain is considerably lessened, and it seems

doubtful to me that such far reaching tariff negotiations will be available to give us the mass entry into some of these markets that is basic to this whole idea of freer trade.
To participate wholeheartedly is all right, provided we are prepared to accept the fact that the degree of success is not as likely to be as marked as we had hoped a year ago. And yet, having embarked on this course, the government has indicated to us that to follow this type of negotiation will require a basic alteration in the industrial complex in Canada. In fact we will probably be required to upset an industrial structure that took four generations to build. In the world of rationalization that will follow these negotiations most, if not all, of our secondary industries will disappear. These industries have been built up under protective tariff walls, and some of them could not survive the lifting of the tariffs and live in the cold winds of international competition.
We would like to hear from the minister, if this were possible, the degree to which our industries will be affected by these tariff concessions. I realize it is perhaps difficult for him to tell us at this stage, but if he can give us some indication of the areas of our economy that will be affected, it would help us in assessing the adequacy of the trade programs.
Having said that, I want to mention a matter raised in the budget, because we have as yet received no answer to it. It is the absence of any sort of government trade adjustment assistance program. If the government is going to ask Canadian industries to bear the brunt of tariff negotiations, then surely our industries and the people employed in them are entitled to a fairly clear statement from the government as to its intentions in the field of trade adjustment assistance. We badly need a strong statement of policy in this regard because the business community is not aware of any strong stand being taken by the government. We need assurance that industries which will be adversely affected will receive financial aid, technical assistance and any other sort of help that is required to take them through the transition stage.
Workers in the plants need to be reassured that their relocation needs will be met, that funds will be available for relocating and training them in the event that their industries are closed. Municipalities also need similar assurance, and so I hope the government will tell the country that it intends to bring into effect a trade adjustment assistance act to take care of the dislocations in our economy which will inevitably follow any widespread tariff concessions in future negotiations. Indeed, it is hard to see where
Supply-Trade and Commerce concessions will be made. After 15 years of tariff negotiations it does not look as though we have much ammunition left in the field of tariff concessions. That is why we would like some indication from the minister at this time on the areas where this type of concession will take place.
As I said earlier, it seems doubtful that the tariff cuts we can make will bring back the type of mass entry into mass markets that is a prerequisite to the whole theory of free trade in the world today.
The real, basic problem we face in Canada-and the minister correctly stated it- is the imbalance between our exports and imports, the release of mass exports of primary products and the lack of exports of manufactured products. The figures we have obtained show that one seventh of our total exports are manufactured goods, and the balance are in primary products. This is one area in which the government should take a very strong stand, and should perhaps examine some of the experiments followed in Europe, particularly in Sweden where a government program amounting almost to partnership and participation with private industry was inaugurated. Gradually Sweden's manufacturing industries have been built up under that program until half its exports are in manufactured products. A strong program of participation by the government with private industry would be beneficial to the Canadian economy.
The other problem that the minister did not deal with, although I hope he will before the debate is finished, is the problem of foreign control of the Canadian economy. Many foreign controlled industries have located in Canada primarily to take advantage of the British preference and of the tariff protection afforded our secondary industry; but if we are to embark on a policy of freer trade and tariff concessions, what will happen to these particular companies, and what plans does the government have in mind to deal with the likelihood that these companies will retreat back into the United States, do their producing there and ship their products into Canada? This, of course, would only accentuate our present difficulties.
I also hope the minister will give us some indication of the impact on the Canadian trade picture of the very extensive campaign being carried out by the Ontario government.
I would like him to assess for us the implication of the "buy Canadian" or "buy Ontario" campaign being conducted by the Ontario government. It seems to me this would have serious implications for the whole policy of free trade.
I would also like the minister to deal with the attempts of the government to have some

Supply-Trade and Commerce of our customers abroad accept quotas on goods they are exporting into Canada. I asked him about this on May 23, and he indicated then that negotiations were taking place. I would like to know how these are progressing and how they fit in with the policy of free trade.
This is not an appropriate time for us to try to lay down an alternative trade program. Perhaps we can do that before the estimates pass; and these are only some of the comments we would like to make on the minister's statement this morning. On the whole, Mr. Chairman, what we heard today does not indicate that the government really has any sort of a trade program. It certainly has given no long range thought to planning. What we were told this morning amounted to many bland platitudes, that there are difficulties, that somehow we will triumph, that the Liberals will carry us through the storm, that they know how to do things, and that they do not have to tell us what their plans are. All we have to do is put our faith in them and everything will be all right. That may be all right from their point of view but it does not satisfy us, in this party. We hope we will have greater clarification on these matters.
As I said at the beginning of my remarks, Mr. Chairman, nothing we heard this morning seems to indicate a long range plan to deal with any of the matters we have raised. There are a host of other matters upon which we would like to comment as we go through the estimates. We did not hear too much this morning of the problem of the underdeveloped nations or the fact that the northern communities are getting richer and the southern communities are remaining relatively poor; and the underdeveloped nations look upon GATT as nothing but a rich man's club that is designed to exclude them from developing their own internal economies. We would like to hear what the government's plans are for the underdeveloped nations.
One hon. member spoke this morning about the need to get into the markets of Europe and to make the necessary concessions. Well, Mr. Chairman, if we look at this matter it does not seem that in Europe they are particularly interested, at this stage, in entering into this type of negotiation; they seem to be insular, self interested and primarily concerned with strengthening their own internal economy at the expense of the rest of the world. If this is true, is it not a dangerous course of action to be taking, to be basing all our program upon the likelihood of freer trade, to be asking the Canadian economy to make basic adjustments and at the same time not be prepared to have in this country

a strong government program of trade adjustment and assistance to compensate industries, communities and workers?
I think this is all we wish to say at this stage, Mr. Chairman, in regard to these estimates. We can raise the other matters as the items come before us.

Mr. Chairman, I merely wish to say a few words about a matter I have set my heart on and which I am sure will be of interest to the minister of commerce (Mr. Sharp) as well as his parliamentary secretary (Mr. Pepin) who, as a former professor at Ottawa university, should be concerned with the problem I am going to raise, namely the metric system.
Would the minister or his parliamentary secretary inform us, at the first opportunity, when item No. 1 of the department of commerce estimates is called, for instance of the government's intention with respect to the application, gradually if possible and without revolutionary changes, of the metric system at the national level?
Besides, in March 1962, quite unexpectedly, the metric system almost grabbed the spotlight at the Canadian conference on education. A scientist of the national research council, Dr. J. T. Henderson, advocated the use of that system. He has pointed out that Great Britain, hoping to enter the common market, intended to adopt that system. A day will come when only a small group of countries will cling to an archaic system of weights and measures. We must act quickly, otherwise we will have to put up with serious troubles on the international markets.
The adoption of the metric system faces serious difficulties. It would probably cost a few billion dollars. We would be compelled to change the scales' graduation, clothes' sizes, length and area measurements, containers' volumes, firearms' caliber, etc.
Those changes would not happen overnight; they could be made gradually. Stores, plants and farms would account mostly for the conversion. Several years would be required for older people to get used to kilogrammes, litres and hectares. Even in France, where the metric system was introduced with the French revolution, there are people who still use old measures.
But for the students, this would be a welcome change. Furthermore, scientists and researchers in laboratories at the national research council for example use the metric system in their work as it is the most logical.

speechtext: Would the hon. member allow me a question? Has he mentioned that the cost of such a system would be of the order of a few billion or a few million dollars?

It would amount to approximately a few million dollars. If I mentioned a few billion, I made a mistake and I thank the hon. member for Berthier-Maski-nonge-Delanaudiere for having called it to my attention.
But Mr. Speaker, in reply to the hon. member, I may say that the application of the metric system would bring in trade worth several million dollars.
If the Canadian government was progressively assuming its responsibilities, it would establish an agency similar to that which is found in the United States, for example, where such an organization is now studying the question, and specially in England, where they have now started to report the weather conditions by using the metric system.
Mr. Speaker, the metric system, however artificial it may seem to us, is logical and of easy application. It allows one to pass rapidly from length to surface and cube, from cube to volume, from volume to weight from weight to price.
Indeed, even a Canadian industrialist has insisted on the urgency of such a reform. In his opinion, the longer the delay, the costlier the change will be.
Mr. Speaker, those were the remarks I wanted to make.
Incidentally, it is interesting to note that India, which is part of the commonwealth, has adopted the metric system.
Surely, he must have noted, as I did, that 95 per cent of the world nations use the metric system.
I know that we will come up against difficulties and that is why I do not suggest that the system be applied overnight. But since education comes under the jurisdiction of the provinces, I think that a federal-provincial conference could be convened on that matter in order to enlist the co-operation of the provinces regarding the adoption of the metric system and even of international road signals.
We could also include the metric system in the school curriculum, since it is now used in all research laboratories and by all scholars in the world, including those in Canada. Incidentally, let me point out that NATO, of which our country is a member, also uses the metric system.
I remember that during the last world war, our allies faced great difficulties because
Supply-Trade and Commerce Canada, among others, did not follow the metric system. In fact, when Canadian forces were advancing through France and building Bailey bridges, several adjustments had to be made because those bridges were built according to English measures, which brought about many difficulties for our allies.
I know that the Minister of Trade and Commerce wants to follow in the footsteps of the previous administration under which our trade growth was staggering. As evidence of this fact, I only need to refer to one of the most sensible statements ever made by the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) when he praised the previous administration for the expansion given to our trade.
I also know that the Minister, conscious of his responsibilities, and having as parliamentary secretary a past and distinguished university professor, will see to it that the problem is given consideration and, following the example set by the United States and England, will establish within his department, a special agency to look into all possibilities in order to adopt gradually the metric system which would give a stimulus to our trade,
