Mr. Chairman, I was most interested in following the speech of the minister this morning. In view of what he had to. say, I would like to make a few brief comments on four of his statements, hoping that he will later in this discussion resolve the statements from platitudes to expressions of plans and policies. I have written down his statements, and if I have them correctly they are as follows: "There is a need for real initiative on behalf of Canadians and producers". Then again: "Canada must respond to basic shifts in trade". Then again: "We can expect keener competition". And lastly: "I am confident that Canadian producers will respond". Mr. Chairman, I am most interested in all four of these statements by the minister this morning, but particularly in the last: "I am confident that Canadian producers will respond".
We have been hearing platitudinous statements of that nature for some considerable time in the House of Commons, but I am most desirous of hearing from the minister whether he will convert that particular platitudinous statement into something of a definite nature whereby we can believe that the producers of Canada are interested, that they will take some initiative and some action. I say that because, although I regret having to make the statement, it is my belief from experience and knowledge that to a great extent there are far too many of our Canadian producers

Supply-Trade and Commerce who still seem to believe that they are in a sellers' market and not in a buyers' market. There are too many who, even if they do recognize that we in Canada are now facing a buyers' market, seem to think that the majority of the responsibility for initiative and planning rests upon the government, and they expect the government to hand them export trade on a silver platter. Somehow or other a change in this attitude must be brought about.
Hon. members may wonder why I feel so strongly in this way and speak so strongly at this time. It is because of the experience which I and three other members of this House of Commons had last year. I fully realize that in Lagos, Nigeria, in the early spring of last year there was a Canadian trade fair, and there is every indication that it was a successful trade fair put on wholly and solely by Canada. But in the late fall of last year an international trade fair was held in Lagos. Nigeria is the most populated country in that section of Africa, having a population of some 42 million. It is a newly developing country. I and three others from this House of Commons, and two members from the Senate, had the opportunity of spending one day at the international trade fair in Lagos. As a Canadian interested in Canadian exports it was one of the most disappointing experiences of my life. The Department of Trade and Commerce of the government of that day made available to Canadian producers a pavilion. The whole of the space in that pavilion was provided free of charge to Canadian producers.
If my information is correct the Department of Trade and Commerce were prepared to pay for the shipment of Canadian produce to be shown in that pavilion. Yet what did we members of the House of Commons and the Senate see at this international trade fair in this Canadian pavilion? There were only two booths with Canadians to explain the exhibits. I can think of three exhibits with no one to explain them; there were just the exhibits themselves. How can producers in Canada hope to get business by sending an exhibit with no one to explain it and no one to take orders? I also remember very distinctly four booths showing exhibits from Ontario, two displaying refrigerators and deep freezers, and one having to do with mechanical equipment, such as pumps. None of these exhibits had anyone from the companies concerned to explain them or show how they worked, or to what use they could be put. I was there at the same time as the lieutenant governor from one of the Nigerian states and the premier of another state, and when they asked who was the

sales representative handling this equipment the answer was that there was not one.
Let me give just two other illustrations, Mr. Chairman. If my memory serves me correctly there are in Ontario millions of pounds of cheddar cheese for which we should like to find a market. This cheese was exhibited at the international fair in Nigeria. Nigerians are not familiar with cheese. To become so they had to pay a shilling to taste a piece. That just does not make sense to me, when you require initiative from Canadian producers to build export markets. What really upset me beyond all that was a power saw produced in British Columbia sitting on a shelf. The people of Nigeria had never seen a power saw and did not know what it was. No one was there to explain, to demonstrate it or to sell it. This is not the way for producers in Canada who have a pavilion supplied to them free by the Department of Trade and Commerce, with shipping costs paid, to expand our export business. That is something which I saw at a Canadian pavilion at the international trade fair in Lagos last November.
It is owing to that experience, Mr. Chairman, and because I honestly believe that there is a real market there in a newly developing country, that I say more is required from the manufacturers and producers in Canada than the expectation that the government will hand them business on a silver platter in a buyers' market. They have responsibilities also. That is the reason why I rose to speak. This experience was only a few months ago. The minister stated that Canada can expect keener competition; that Canada must respond to basic shifts in trade.
The minister followed that up by saying there was a need for real initiative on the part of Canadian producers. He was confident, he said, that Canadian producers would respond to what was demanded of them. Well, I wonder if the hon. gentleman would give us some indication as to how he came to that conclusion and what policies and plans he has in mind in order to activate some of our producers in Canada whose business must be maintained and expanded, not only in their own interest but in order to be able to provide employment in Canada.
I note that for the balance of the present year the Department of Trade and Commerce is taking part in only two exhibitions in the United Kingdom-an international packing exhibition in London from September 4 to 12 and the building trades exhibition also in London from November 13 to 27. It is true some thought is being given to taking part in an exhibition called the Belfast ideal homes exhibition in September of 1964. I want to plead with the minister that he

should follow through with his project of activating industry. On my way back from Africa last December I met with the British Columbia trade commissioner at British Columbia House in London. I found very little was being done at that time by either the lumber industry or the building industry of Canada to show at these exhibitions what Canada can do and what Canada possesses in the way of modern building materials. I hope that in the past few months this situation has been corrected. I trust the minister will go beyond platitudes and give us information as to the plans he and his department have in mind so see that we do take action, and that all this action does not come from the government side; because responsibility for the expansion of our markets in the interest of Canadian employment also rests with industry itself. Unless industry is told bluntly and emphatically to get off its backside and accept that responsibility, I am afraid we shall have difficulty in meeting what the minister has called the shifting changes of trade patterns throughout the world.

Canadian industry is faced with almost insurmountable obstacles in trying to compete in the highly industrialized and heavily populated areas of Europe. No one is suggesting that we should ignore the opportunities in this market. Supply-Trade and Commerce found in association with the nations of South America and other emerging nations of the world.
At the close of world war II, Canada enjoyed for a brief period the right to claim third place in the trade of the world. That situation rapidly evaporated with the recovery of industrial activity in Europe. The unemployment situation that resulted from the slowdown in Canadian trade at that time has, to a large extent, remained with us despite the greater numbers absorbed into the labour market as a result of the normal growth of demand on the domestic market for goods. The present government has provided us with a number of proposals designed to improve employment. The previous government was also responsible for a number of measures which were helpful. I would be remiss in my duties here if I did not point out that the attitude of the government is somewhat different from that which has been expressed by the minister today. This is particularly true in regard to the need for Canadian industries to achieve an increased measure of efficiency and economy of operation. The imposition of a sales tax of 11 per cent on production machinery and building materials appears to be a factor adverse to the increase in production for which the minister expressed hope in his remarks today.
I imagine the future of Canada as a trading nation will depend largely on the measure of boldness and decision with which we approach our target. When one takes a look at the legislation which has been placed on the order paper, and when one

Supply-Trade and Commerce considers the provisions made in the budget itself, I would say that neither is good enough to solve our problems.
I believe that the people of my area and some other parts of Canada as well want the government to be made aware of the fact that an effort must be launched to arrest the continuing rise in what is already a high priced economy. I hope the minister will continue to direct his attention and that of the department to the "buy Canadian" campaign. We have a great domestic market in Canada. We have been buying more goods from other countries than we should. Buying Canadian goods is one of the things that Canadians can do for themselves and perhaps with continued encouragement we will finally be able to put more Canadians to work at the task of producing goods to satisfy consumer demands.
I was pleased to hear the minister say that expansion is now under way in the Canadian economy. During the past several years the attention of the former government led by the present Leader of the Opposition was focused on trying to extend that expansion, and one of the matters that received their attention was power development and the energy resources of Canada generally. The devaluation of the Canadian dollar, following as it did so many years after the devaluation of the currencies of other countries, brought the products of Canadian industry more closely and intimately in competition with the products of other countries in world markets. These actions were taken by the government led by my leader. I might say that the decisions were not easy ones to take. However, they have already been of great assistance to the primary and secondary industries of this country.
I believe I should say a word or two about grain marketing. My constituency is one of the great grain producing areas of Canada and was one of the first to focus attention on the quality of Canadian grain when the late Seager Wheeler of Rosthern won the world wheat championship three times in a row. That was a long time ago. I notice


that the export figures for rye and oats this year are above those of a year ago. The price of Canadian wheat in world markets today has reached a level in excess of what would have been imagined possible only a few short years ago.
One of the factors involved in this, of course, has been the credit sales that have been made and among those sales are those that have been made to red China. We on this side of the house believed that when those sales were made it was the breaking of the sod in an effort to supply Canadian grain to those areas where people were hungry and where there was a need. We believed that resulting from that agreement there should follow a greatly increased impetus on the part of our own Department of Trade and Commerce, and also in the markets of the world, that would see an increasing measure of Canadian grain going to such countries. I will not say anything further with regard to the agreement or the grain position at this time. I know this matter is being discussed in other places and perhaps the less said at this time the better.
Another problem that concerns the people of western Canada has to do with the oil industry and the oil market in this country. We would like to see greater use being made of the oil resources to be found in western Canada. When we look at the imports of oil into Canada we sometimes wonder whether all is being done that could be done in that regard.
I do not intend to say anything further. I know that the Secretary of State was over here a little while ago with a big smile on his face hoping that we would not take too long. He wants to get on with the business of the house. There will be other opportunities in other debates to deal with some of these matters. Finally, may I say that I believe that the future of Canada as a great trading nation perhaps lies more with the underdeveloped nations than with the other nations of the world. There is a great opportunity for us there, not only with regard to agricultural products but also industrial and heavy machinery products that our people can produce.

Supply-Trade and Commerce
However, my interest in this subject is mostly as a representative of an agricultural constituency, and my concern is mostly with agricultural imports and exports. I am particularly interested in the export of grain. Our exports over the last five years were quite a bit higher than the exports during the term of the previous Liberal government. This was a source of great satisfaction to all of our farmers. At the moment the situation does not look quite so good. I am not saying this has anything to do with the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, far from it. However, the prospects for a crop this year are extremely good. As a result of this, we may be faced with surplus grain. Since the Canadian wheat board comes under the jurisdiction of the Department of Trade and Commerce, I should like to bring to the attention of the minister the great concern of the people in the three western provinces.
I should like particularly to direct the minister's attention to one matter, and that is the quota system as it exists in our provinces. I have before me a little map which shows that my constituency of Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale is one that has hardly any areas on a 12-bushel quota. As a matter of fact, I did bring this to the attention of the minister earlier, and I am sure he will take steps to see what can be done about it. Of the 67 delivery points in my constituency, I find that there are about 50 that are on an eight- or ten-bushel quota and there are only 16 that are on a 12-bushel quota. This brings me to a point I raised not so long ago when I introduced a bill. I am not going to discuss that bill at the moment, but I should like to direct the attention of the minister to the great need for storage space in my area. Previous governments which investigated this situation were told that they could have grain terminals built in this area to expedite the export of grain through the port of Churchill.
At the moment grain exports through the port of Churchill are at a very low figure, amounting to approximately 20 million or 25 million bushels. My area is one of the closest to this port, being only about 600 miles from it. If we had a terminal in our area we could have expedited the export of grain through Churchill, thus alleviating not only the surplus position in which my constituency finds itself but also increase the total amount exported through this port. This is an important consideration because producers save approximately seven cents a bushel on grain which is exported through Churchill to Liverpool.
Another matter pertaining to the same problem is that in the very near future we will be faced with an abandonment of railroads. In my constituency many farmers will

be left without storage facilities because of this abandonment. All indications are that the crop this year will be very heavy and farmers in my constituency will not have storage space. Because of this, the terminal which I have suggested to the minister would be a great thing.
At present we have two government terminals, one in Saskatoon and the other in Edmonton, but over the years they have been used only to half their capacity. One reason is that during a surplus year private grain companies are reluctant to have grain stored at government terminals because they lose revenue on account of that. This is a very serious matter. I know I am not disclosing any new information to the minister, but in view of the seriousness of the matter I ask him to make strong representations to the government.
In conclusion I wish to say the farmers in my constituency are looking forward to an active approach in the selling of grain. During the past four or five years the previous minister in charge of the Canadian wheat board made very good efforts, as a result of which we were able to dispose of our surplus grain. With active efforts on the part of the present minister I believe markets can be found for our grain. If the right approach is taken, the minister will be able to see that more grain is sold to the customers we had over the last four or five years.

As long as we are selling Canadian flour to any nation it is assumed, and I think it is pretty safe to assume, that we use 100 per cent Canadian wheat to produce that flour. But when we get into the position where we are exporting wheat to be milled in other countries and then transshipped to the ultimate consumer through international trade, we get ourselves into a less competitive position with regard to supplying the raw material.
I am a little disturbed about this. I said that I do not wish to take up a great deal of time now; but there have been cases where new mills have been established in

some of the countries to which we were supplying the flour. Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to keep the committee very long. I am sorry to disappoint my old friend the Secretary of State who has been urging us to hurry up, but there are one or two things I would like to say on vote No. 1 in the hope that I may be able to elicit some comment on the points I intend to raise from the Minister of Trade and Commerce.

I am always a little disturbed when I hear public men, as I have been hearing them all my adult life, intone in almost reverent terms the phrase that Canada is a great trading nation. This is always good for a round of applause, of course, but very few people stop to consider just what the end result of having been a great trading nation may be. This morning the minister told us quite plainly that after many decades of being a great trading nation in our own estimation we are in this position, that we have been relying either on duty free or low duty agreements for the sale of our primary products, and that Canada is one of the world's largest importers of manufactured goods. In addition to that we have 60 per cent or more of our industry and resources owned by non-Canadians.
I think that in considering this whole question of trade we should first of all decide just what is our purpose in world trade. I think we have to distinguish between the purposes of the Canadian community as a whole and the purposes of certain Canadians. Obviously one has only to think for a moment or two to realize that there is only one purpose in external trade that we could have as a community, and that is to supplement our own economy. There would be no other purpose or gain that you and I as citizens of Canada could achieve from it. On the other hand there are Canadian citizens who do have another purpose, a much more narrow purpose though quite legitimate one, and that is the purpose of making money by the sale of Canadian primary products.
I believe a lot of our confusion arises from the rather careless use of terms. We speak of Canada's exports. To my knowledge there are only two classes of goods which come into that category. One is wheat, which has been dealt with quite extensively this afternoon and the suggestion made that the methods by which Canada sells wheat should now be extended to take in manufactured products as well; and the other commodity, of course, is uranium, which we are having some difficulty in selling. Apart from that we have the situation of a number of Canadians engaged in selling commodities on the world's markets.
I am fully aware of the theory, if it could be dignified as that, on the division of labour throughout the world. This, of course, is something one should aim at, at some time in the future. But I would point out that this question of trading on the world's markets cannot be considered in purely economic terms, or rather in the statistical economic terms in which it is usually considered. The world as a whole is not going to be able to meet its requirements for the goods of the
Supply-Trade and Commerce abundant life for the greatly increased population which every demographer tells us we can expect in the next 50 years, unless every part of the world is fully developed to its utmost capacity. And we are not going to do that so long as we stick out our chests and say that we are a great trading nation, overlooking the fact that what we are is a nation which has sold ever and ever greater proportions of its resources, both natural and manufactured, to non-residents. We are a nation which is dependant on a stream of exports of primary products with very little effort having been spent on the development of our secondary industries to satisfy the needs of our own people.
I think it is illuminating to realize the stage at which a nation decides that it is all in favour of free trade. I know that even to suggest that some qualification may be required about free trade is almost heresy, if not sacrilege. I know quite well there is something moral about free trade and something immoral about any obstacles in the way of free trade. It is rather curious how these moral attachments came about. I think we should remember that the concept of free trade arose in the Manchester school of liberalism within the sound of the whirring spindles of the Lancashire textile industry. It was a very sound proposition for those people. It is interesting to note that the United States of America, which has quite recently reached the position of having the most productive economy in the world, has now suddenly come to the conclusion that there is something moral in free trade on which she turned her back during the whole of her years of development. No economy was ever developed behind such high walls as that of the United States. The development has now taken place, and suddenly we find a new apostle for free trade.
I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that Canada has to consider her position in the light of these developments. I do not think there can be much doubt that if a real liberalizing program of trade were to be undertaken with no holds barred, at the present time Canada would find herself in an increasingly difficult position; and unless at the same time we were taking steps to develop the economic facilities required for the satisfaction of as large a part of our own needs as possible, then we would be relatively in the same position as the undeveloped areas of the world about which the minister was speaking this afternoon. We should not be deceived by the fact that we are a fairly comfortable and affluent undeveloped area of the world. It is only a question of degree as between the position of Canadians and the positions of the inhabitants of the new emerging

Supply-Trade and Commerce countries in that they too are dependent entirely at the present time on the sale of raw materials and primary products in world markets, and are having the greatest difficulties in developing their own secondary industries.
I suggest, sir, as I said earlier, that it is absolutely essential that before we embark on any vast unlimited campaign of liberalization of trade we should keep in mnid the fact that the world is going to require something more from Canada than merely a storehouse of primary products; that the demands of the ever increasing world population are going to make it necessary for Canada and every other part of the world not yet properly developed to become developed to its fullest capacity in order to satisfy as much of its own needs as possible, and to place on the world's markets the surpluses which may accrue. I think that is our domestic problem.
I also think we share in another and perhaps more important world problem. My colleague from Danforth touched on it briefly earlier this afternoon and I should like to explore it a little further. It is the question of an expanding economy in a world in which exchange difficulties are becoming ever more critical and ever more frequent. I think we must bear in mind in fact that the two great reserve currencies of the world, the dollar and the pound, are now in a dangerously weakened position and may well become weaker still, unless some steps are taken in the international field to overcome this difficulty. My colleague made particular reference this afternoon to some comments which were made not long ago by Mr. Harold Wilson. Mr. Wilson was, of course, merely echoing the views of many other economists who have pointed out in recent years the dangers which lie ahead in the world today unless we can establish some better basis for international liquidity than the present international monetary fund. Unless that fund is enabled to move into a new sphere of activity as, in effect, an international central bank, we shall experience recurring exchange crises which will come about precisely as the developed areas of the world begin to expand. We shall find that the less developed areas of the world will not be able to develop secondary industries. They will find themselves with a continually declining price level for their primary products and will not be in a position to establish secondary manufacturing industries, because the price of being able to sell their primary products will be the acceptance of manufactured goods from the developed countries.

I was pleased to hear in the hon. gentleman's introductory statement the comments he had to make on the activities of the Canadian government travel bureau.
I have also been pleased to note that since he assumed the portfolio he has shown a keen appreciation of the economic significance of the activities of this very important branch of government. I suppose I might term my remarks today somewhat of a swan song because up until last fall the branch was a part of the responsibility of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. At that time, largely because of the impressive upsurge in the tourist industry, the work of the Canadian government travel bureau was transferred back to the Department of Trade and Commerce. This was recognition, which I feel came far too late, of the economic value of this important activity.
It has not come about accidentally that tourism is now recognized as an important segment of Canada's economic activity. I want to take this opportunity to pay tribute to the director of the bureau, the assistant director and the excellent staff associated 28902-5-121
Supply-Trade and Commerce with them. They have worked hard and diligently and have planned carefully over recent years with the objective in mind of making tourism the significant industry they have long realized it could become, provided it was given support by government.
During the past five years a deliberate program of tourist promotion was embarked upon. It was not only a matter of encouraging the activities of the travel bureau but also involved the co-ordination of all aspects of the Canadian economy which might be identified with the encouragement of the tourist industry, such as the construction of roads, the roads to resources program, the completion of the trans-Canada highway, the establishment of a network of air terminals adequate to meet the demands of modern air transportation, the development, refurbishing and expansion of our national parks system and the development of historic sites and monuments which are always major tourist attractions. We only have to point to the impact of the changing of the guard ceremony on parliament hill, which all hon. members recognize has become one of our major tourist attractions. Small business loans were another feature of this broad planning program to encourage the development of the tourist industry.
Then there is also the newly developed interest in that huge area north of the 60th parallel, northern Canada. Here too it has been recognized that the tourist industry is one of its major economic assets and as a result of the activities over the past years it can now be said that tourism in both the Northwest Territories and the Yukon territory is their second most important industry.
As a result of these activities it can be said-in fact it has been stated many times- that the year 1962 can be designated as the year of the tourist. As the minister said in his opening remarks, for the first time dollar income from the tourist industry reached a level of more than half a billion dollars. Now we press on to the next five years and I am certain that the attitude displayed by the minister will ensure that the program announced at the federal-provincial tourist conference in Ottawa last October will be achieved. At that time it was estimated that by 1967 the tourist industry would realize a dollar income of $1 billion a year. This estimate was based on the continuing expansion and rapid upsurge last year and also on the impact that will be made by the celebration of Canada's centennial.
It is also predicated, of course, on the degree of success anticipated from Canada's invasion of a hitherto unexploited market, that of the United Kingdom and Europe. As

Trade and Commerce hon. members know, the decision was made last year to move into this market. We had a very auspicious opening in the city of London near Trafalgar square last September and already there has been an encouraging response from that initiative. I heartily concur with him and I am sure he has come to that conclusion having had an opportunity to realize the tremendous progress that has been made in this economic activity and because he is now fully aware of the buoyancy of the Canadian economy in the last year. One final word, Mr. Chairman. These things cannot be achieved without broad co-operation in many quarters. I have already referred to the quality of the staff of the Canadian government travel bureau. These men have established very cordial and friendly relations with the provincial departments. I think that one of the happiest contacts a federal minister can have with his provincial counterparts occurs during the annual federal-provincial conference on tourism. This is an atmosphere that has been cultivated over the years. The spirit of co-operation has been well established and is recognized as being important because tourism is important to all segments of Canada.
Then there are the activities of the Canadian tourist association, a voluntary group which has served Canada well in promoting this important industry. It has had such illustrious Canadians identified with it as John Fisher who is now in charge of Canada's centennial planning. The national energy board is now in its fourth year of operation. Its functions may be classified broadly as regulatory and advisory, and the general nature of its activities is reflected in the make up of its personnel which are predominantly professional and technical.
On the regulatory side, the board is interested in the interprovincial and international movement of hydrocarbons by pipe line and the exportation of electrical power. Its regulatory functions may be divided into classes of action which are quasi judicial, in that they establish or vary rights and interests in property and those which are administrative.
The quasi judicial functions include the issuance of certificates of public convenience and necessity for international power lines and for interprovincial and international pipe lines for the transmission of oil and gas; the

Supply-Trade and Commerce issuance of licences for the exportation and importation of gas and the exportation of electrical power; the authorization of pipe line companies to expropriate land; the authorization of crossings by or of pipe lines; and the regulation of the traffic, tolls and tariffs of pipe lines under its jurisdiction.
It might be of interest to the house to know that last year the board held 11 public hearings which resulted in the issuance of certificates and licences. In addition the board is empowered to approve the construction of certain pipe lines and pipe line facilities by exempting such construction from certificate proceedings, and in this connection the board issued 18 such orders for gas and oil pipe line facilities. Some 98 orders were issued under various other regulatory sections of the National Energy Board Act.
The regulatory functions of an administrative character include those having to do with the protection of public safety as it may be affected by pipe lines, and the miscellaneous matters involved in ensuring that pipe line companies under the jurisdiction of the board comply with the terms of their acts of incorporation and with the provisions of the act. The staff of the board conducts field inspections relating to the safety of pipe lines under its jurisdiction. One of the chief provisions of the act relating to safety has to do with the issuance of crossing orders, and in this connection last year the board issued some 295 such orders. In addition the board issued 28 leave-to-open orders for pipe lines under its jurisdiction. The board is currently participating in the work of a Canadian standards association committee to establish a Canadian code for the design, construction and operation of oil and gas pipe lines.
An increasing portion of the board's responsibility relates to its advisory functions under part II of the act, which charge the board with studying and keeping under review all matters relating to energy falling within the jurisdiction of this parliament. In pursuance of this obligation, the board has continued the preparation of detailed supply and demand forecasts relating to energy, and indeed just today I authorized the publication of a short term forecast. In co-operation with other agencies of government it has endeavoured to establish more comprehensive and more accurate statistical series for energy. It has been engaged in the preparation of a short term energy forecast, in the course of which it has consulted federal and provincial agencies and industry groups.
The board has participated in arrangements for studies of a national power grid and in studies of the feasibility of developing certain remote hydroelectric power resources. The advisory work of the board will be intensified

as we move further in the development of joint energy studies with the United States, concerning which I reported to the house a short time ago.
I mentioned a moment ago the regulatory function of the board in connection with tolls and tariffs relating to the operation of pipe lines under the board's jurisdiction. To prepare itself for any formal action which it might be called upon to take in this respect, the board has prepared and prescribed uniform classification of accounts for gas and oil pipe line companies, which provide uniformity in accounting practices and which facilitate the board's review of the financial records of companies under its jurisdiction.

May I take this opportunity to thank hon. members for their contributions to the discussion of these estimates and for their kind words, which are greatly appreciated by a new minister. I should like to comment on the remarks of various speakers in reverse order, which may not suit hon. members who spoke first, but which will help me in recalling what they said.
I attempted to answer some of the questions put to me by the hon. member for Lapointe. The hon. member for Macleod and the hon. member for Brandon-Souris made some comments about the importance of the tourist industry, with which I am in full agreement. I would like to thank the former minister, who at one time had responsibility for the Canadian travel bureau, for his words of encouragement, and also to commend him for the work that he did in promoting the tourist industry in this country when that bureau was under his jurisdiction. I can assure him that I took over the travel bureau in excellent shape. I do hope we shall be able to carry forward its work and that we shall attain those objectives which I stated, and which

I hope will result in there being even greater encouragement to the tourist industry than under his administration.
I might add that I had the privilege, when I was in London, of visiting the travel bureau office which is just off Trafalgar square. Perhaps the house will be interested to know that the results of the new efforts made to promote the tourist trade in the United Kingdom, have been excellent. The travel bureau inserted a series of advertisements for the first time in United Kingdom newspapers, promoting travel to Canada, and in the first week received 10,000 inquiries, which was really a very remarkable result from a single series of advertisements.
The hon. member for Pictou referred to the importance of export credits, and I want to say to him that the government is fully aware of the importance of making export credits available, particularly for the export of those heavy industrial goods that he was talking about. I hope he will not think I am speaking too politically when I say it was under the previous Liberal administration that these policies were first introduced and developed, and I am happy that these initial efforts, which proved successful at the time, have been carried forward. I hope we shall continue to expand our exports and that these credit facilities will help us in that respect.
I am also conscious, of course, of the importance of the South American market. I happen to have spent some time in Brazil when I was in private business, and I am aware of the tremendous potential. I am also aware of the great difficulties of doing business in those countries, and about the importance therefore of having credit facilities to enable those countries to go on purchasing goods from abroad during their period of rapid development.
The hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands made a very interesting series of comments about trade policy. I shall not attempt to answer all his arguments, but I would like to put forward a few comments upon the thesis or theses that he presented. First of all he said that I, like so many other speakers, had spoken about Canada being a great trading nation. He somehow felt that this had been said too many times.
I do not think it can be said too many times, and may I suggest to him the reason I said it, and this I draw particularly to his attention, is that we have a high standard of living because we are a great trading nation. This is the reason that 18 million people are able to exploit the resources of Canada so efficiently. Because we have foreign markets to which we can sell the surplus we
Supply-Trade and Commerce create, we have our high standard of living, the second or third highest among the countries of the world.
He also spoke about the desirability of promoting industrialization. The reason I as Minister of Trade and Commerce, and the government as a whole, are profoundly interested in the success of the trade negotiations that are about to begin, is that we believe it is only through successful trade negotiations that we shall be able to achieve the kind of industrialization we all want to have in this country.
One of the main reasons this country is an exporter of primary materials and foodstuffs to such a high degree is the structure of foreign tariffs. It is because in the United States there are very high tariffs against manufactured goods and very low tariffs against raw materials and foodstuffs. The purpose of the trade negotiations that are under way today, as far as we are concerned, is to reduce those high tariffs on manufactured goods so that Canadian manufacturers have an opportunity of getting into foreign markets with their products, not only in the United States but in Europe and Britain. I really am quite surprised that the hon. member should be guilty of the sort of interpretation of history that he gave, because I would have thought, to judge from some of his other remarks, that he might have a rather more sophisticated view of these matters. But I suggest to him that the reason the United States developed as a great manufacturing nation was not because of the external tariffs around that country but because of the existence within that country of the world's greatest common market. The United States is still the world's greatest common market. It is because, when those 13 colonies were formed, they decided to form a common market that the United States today has become the greatest industrial nation in the world. It is not because of their external tariffs; it is because of the lack of internal tariffs among the states.
The other point I would like to emphasize -and this arises not only in connection with What the hon. gentleman said but in connection with what has been said by other hon. members-is that no one on this side of the house has ever proposed that Canada should enter into unlimited trade negotiation.
In the statement I made to the house after returning from London and Geneva I made it quite plain that Canada was going to bargain for access to foreign markets, for which we were willing to pay equivalent value. Our negotiating position is that we will pay for what we get. This, surely, is the essence of anyone's bargaining position and it must

Supply-Trade and Commerce be the position that is taken by Canada. We did not accept for Canada the pattern of trade concessions that the United States is proposing or that Britain is willing to accept or, we hope, that the European common market is willing to accept. We said that would not be suitable for Canada, and therefore we insisted upon the resolution on which these negotiations are based containing a clause which says that countries in our position shall offer concessions of equivalent value, not necessarily of a linear character.

That does not mean that it would not be sensible to move toward a metric system, but I think it places some limitation on the rate at which we can proceed.
I now come to the remarks made by the hon. member for Danforth. I should like to comment on one point he made: An apparent conflict between economic planning and freer trade. My view, and I am sure it is the view shared by all those who have had some practical experience in these matters, is that for a country like Canada that is so heavily dependant upon trade, and likely to remain heavily dependant upon trade, economic planning must take into account the realities of our international position. Any idea that there is a conflict between these two objectives is, I think, based on a misunderstanding of the nature of true economic planning, or upon a misunderstanding of our position in the world. There is and can be no conflict. These two objectives of planning our activities and promoting trade must go hand in hand, so I really do not think that most of what he said really bore on the problem that faces our country today.
He also made some statements to the effect that I did not make a good case for freer trade. Perhaps I did not. I will grant that. However, as I said in replying to the hon. member for Nanaimo-Cowichan-The Islands, I do believe that the objective of the round of trade negotiations which is just about to begin is to promote the industrialization of Canada. The case for freer trade is that it enables us to raise our standard of living. Otherwise we would not engage in it. We are not doing this because of adherence to any Manchester school or because we have any predilections for any particular economic theory. We are doing it for good practical reasons, namely to promote the welfare of Canadians.
Now, I should like to comment on the remarks of the hon. member for Edmonton West who opened the discussion. While I did not deal in my opening remarks with more than one subject, it was not because I could not have spoken all day about the activities of the Department of Trade and Commerce. I wish to assure him that as

Supply-Trade and Commerce minister I intend to carry forward the work of trade promotion just as actively as the work of trade negotiation and policy. I have been reviewing the activities of the department over the past few years, during which time some very good work was done in the field of trade promotion. But you cannot go on doing the same things over and over again, and it will be my objective to adapt the trade promotion program of the department to meet the needs of the coming year, and not to copy the program of previous years. I intend to have regional trade conferences across the country. These will differ in form, perhaps differ in membership. I intend to continue the promotion of trade through international conferences, but perhaps not in exactly the way it was done before. There were some weaknesses in the previous programs as well as some very strong points. But I can assure the hon. gentleman that the work of trade promotion will be carried on just as actively, and perhaps even more effectively, than in the past.
I do not agree with the hon. gentleman that the failure of the United Kingdom to enter the European common market has made the current negotiations abortive. I think it would have been better if Britain had been able to negotiate herself successfully into the European common market. Then there would have been even greater scope for trade negotiations under the Kennedy round. There are nevertheless great opportunities still available. The best evidence of that is that the strongest advocates of the Kennedy round are not the Americans but the British. At the Geneva talks the United Kingdom said that they were prepared to go as far as any other country in the world in linear tariff cuts. They took this view for obvious reasons. Not having joined the common market by negotiation they now want to reduce the tariff barriers against them in Europe, in the United States and in all other countries. So this could be a very important round of tariff negotiations and I believe we should, as I said, do everything possible to ensure that the negotiations succeed.
Finally, the hon. gentleman spoke about the value of expanding our trade with the Caribbean. I should like to agree with him. This is an area in which we have had traditional ties over many years. It is an area of great potential and one in which Canada has already done some very useful things. I am sure the hon. member is aware of the extent of our trade relations with this area. In 1961, for example, we imported from the British West Indies $84 million worth of goods, mainly sugar and bauxite. This is one of the largest exports of that area; we are one of its biggest customers. Our exports to that

area were somewhat less. So this is an area which is dependant upon Canada and it is one in which we can take advantage of the good will and of the excellent relations which have existed in the past to develop even closer trade to the mutual benefit of both the West Indies and ourselves. We have trade commission offices in Kingston, Jamaica, and Port of Spain. We are sending an appliance and houseware mission to visit Barbados and Trinidad during October and November of this year. This is part of the program of promoting better relations and closer ties with that area. Over the last five years we have granted $2 million in aid, and $2 million have been requested for 1963-64 to supply economic assistance. Many Canadian teachers and technical advisers have gone to that area. I expect that more will go. I could give many more instances of the influence of Canada in that area.
I would like to conclude by saying once again how much I have appreciated the cooperation of the committee this afternoon.

Item agreed to.

speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I wonder if before you proceed to any other item of business, Mr. Speaker, the house will permit me to say just a word. I want first of all, to thank all hon. members for the wonderful co-operation we have had today. In the second place, I wonder if I might be permitted, because of an engagement which I have, to announce the business for next week or for the part of next week I am in a position to announce it for, that is Monday and Tuesday. I have explained to hon. gentlemen opposite why I do not want to go beyond that at the moment.
There is, I think, general understanding that on Monday we would take the two resolutions pertaining to the two northwest territories. The debate will be very brief and we do not intend to proceed beyond the resolution stage and the first reading of the bills. The reason is that certain arrangements

of long standing have been made-the hon. member for Brandon-Souris, in particular, will be familiar with them. There is a meeting of the Northwest Territories council arranged for next week and the commissioner is anxious to have the bills available for consideration by the council because of important constitutional developments which are likely to result from these bills. So if there could be an understanding that perhaps one speaker from each party would take part in the debate, so that we might get these things through in a reasonable time, it would be the government's desire to go ahead with those items.
Then we intend to take the Atlantic development board bill and the economic council bill. If there should be any other item required before Tuesday is over we would call the resolution respecting the Department of Agriculture. I should like to confer with hon. gentlemen opposite some time on Tuesday with respect to the business for the rest of the week.
Having announced the business for Monday and Tuesday, I wonder if the house would consider the desirability of forgoing the private members' hour today and adjourning. We have in this building as a guest with us the prime minister of Australia, Sir Robert Menzies. I understand a reception is being given for this distinguished visitor who first visited Canada and spoke in this house 22 years ago-there is nothing significant about the 22 years. It occurred to me that since we have accomplished so much in the last two days perhaps hon. members would like to have the opportunity of meeting the prime minister of Australia for a little longer. I just put forward this suggestion realizing it would need unanimous consent.

As far as we are concerned we would be very happy to adjourn and give all hon. members an opportunity to meet this distinguished visitor who is an old friend of Canada. The hour is rather late and it would be awkward for some hon. members to stay here too long, so I think it might be helpful if we were to adjourn as soon as possible.
We in this group would be quite amenable to accepting the suggestion made by the Secretary of State.

I should like to take this opportunity of speaking on behalf of our group and to express our agreement with the suggestion which has been made. I do so for two reasons. I have had the honour of meeting the prime minister of Australia both in Canada and in Australia. The second reason is that I happen to be half kangaroo, my

mother having been born in Australia. That is why I sought the privilege of rising on behalf of this group to accept the suggestion which has been made.

May I be permitted to rise on a question of privilege? I gave an answer today which was incorrect and I would like to take the earliest possible opportunity to correct it. When I was asked by the hon. member for Lapointe how many bilingual employees there were in the department I gave the figure accurately, 318, but I said that was excluding the dominion bureau of statistics. When I gave the figure for the total number of employees in the department, I gave a figure which included the bureau of statistics. The correct figures are: 318 bilingual employees in the Department of Trade and Commerce, excluding the dominion bureau of statistics, out of 1,860.
